title: 台風 23日から沖縄先島諸島に接近
body:
大型で猛烈な台風30号は、今後沖縄の南を北西に進み、23日(金)から24日(土)にかけて非常に強い勢力で沖縄の先島諸島に接近する見込みです。暴風や高波、大雨に厳重な警戒が必要です。また、台風周辺の湿った空気が流れ込むため、西日本から東日本に延びる前線の活動が活発化し、台風接近前から大雨となる恐れがあります。26日(月)頃からは台風が西日本に近づくため、風が強まり、高波や高潮の恐れがあります。
22日(木)3時現在、台風30号は大型で猛烈な勢力を維持しています。中心の気圧は905ヘクトパスカル、中心付近の最大風速は55メートル、最大瞬間風速は80メートルとなっています。台風30号は今後沖縄の南を北西に進み、23日(金)から24日(土)頃にかけて非常に強い勢力で石垣島など先島諸島に接近する見込みです。その後、台風は急カーブして、26日(月)頃から西日本へ近づくでしょう。27日(火)には日本海で温帯低気圧に変わる見込みです。
先島諸島では23日(金)から24日(土)は暴風となり、一部の住家が倒壊する恐れもある猛烈な風が吹く見込みです。海上では波の高さが11メートルに達するような猛烈なしけとなるでしょう。台風の雨雲がかかり、警報級の大雨となる見込みです。・風の予想22日(木)に予想される風向・最大風速(最大瞬間風速)沖縄本島地方　18メートル(30メートル)大東島地方　　15メートル(25メートル)宮古島地方　　23メートル(35メートル)八重山地方　　23メートル(35メートル)23日(金)に予想される風向・最大風速(最大瞬間風速)沖縄本島地方　18メートル(30メートル)大東島地方　　15メートル(25メートル)宮古島地方　　25メートル(35メートル)八重山地方　　40メートル(55メートル)24日(土)に予想される風向・最大風速(最大瞬間風速)沖縄本島地方　18メートル(30メートル)大東島地方　　15メートル(25メートル)宮古島地方　　25メートル(35メートル)八重山地方　　40メートル(55メートル)・雨の予想22日(木)6時から23日(金)6時までに予想される24時間降水量は多い所で沖縄本島地方　120ミリ宮古島地方　　80ミリ八重山地方　　150ミリその後、23日(金)6時から24日(土)6時までに予想される24時間降水量は多い所で宮古島地方　　120ミリ八重山地方　　300ミリその後、24日(土)6時から25日(日)6時までに予想される24時間降水量は多い所で八重山地方　　150ミリ先島諸島では頑丈な建物の中に移動するとともに屋内では窓から離れるなど暴風に厳重な警戒が必要です。うねりを伴う高波に厳重に警戒し、海岸付近には近づかないようにしてください。また、土砂災害に厳重に警戒し、低い土地の浸水、河川の増水や氾濫に警戒してください。
23日(金)頃から西日本に秋雨前線が延びるでしょう。前線に向かって台風周辺の暖かく湿った空気が流れ込み、前線の活動が活発化しそうです。九州から近畿は雨が降り、九州を中心に非常に激しい雨が降って、大雨となる所があるでしょう。24日(土)から26日(月)頃は前線が東日本まで延び、九州から北陸にかけて大雨となり、九州や中国、北陸では警報級の大雨となる恐れもあります。関東も本降りの雨となるでしょう。特に、26日(月)頃には台風が近づく西日本では風も強まり、大しけや警報級の高潮となる恐れもあります。最新の台風情報にご注意ください。

title: G7TV会議を首相欠席 与野党波紋
body: 21日で政権発足から1年を迎えた高市早苗首相が今月2日の先進7カ国（G7）テレビ会議を欠席し、与野党に波紋を広げている。首相は回線接続のための業者の手配が間に合わなかったと釈明。事実なら緊急時に国際会議に即応できない恐れがあり、政府の危機管理能力が問われることになる。外交や防衛に力を入れる政権のイメージも低下しかねないだけでなく、政府・与党内には首相の説明を疑う向きもある。テレビ会議は2日午後9時半から30分間、イラン情勢や米欧の燃料高について協議。7カ国のうち欠席したのは首相とバーナム英首相のみで、日本は外務省の遠藤和也外務審議官が代理出席した。外務省によると、2023年以降は歴代首相が出席している。首相は欠席理由について、16日の参院予算委員会で「開催時間が直前までわからなかった」「大きなディスプレーを使うのに事業者に頼むが間に合わなかった」と説明。一方、主催国のフランス大統領府は「数日前に案内した」としている。開催時間が不明でも、回線を接続できなかったことが欠席理由なら、政府の準備不足との指摘は免れない。有事の国際会議にも対応できない恐れがある。首相経験者は「国際会議はいつも急に行われる。機器の不備なら大失態」と驚く。首相の説明に懐疑的な声も上がる。官邸関係者は「回線を準備できないわけがない。最初から欠席するつもりだったはずだ」と憤る。首相はこの日、午後8時ごろまで自民党の麻生太郎副総裁ら党幹部と公邸で会食後、所信表明演説に手を入れていた。首相周辺は「出席する意味がない会議だった」と打ち明ける。首相のリスク管理が疑問視されるのは初めてではない。今年2月28日にはイラン攻撃の第1報後に県知事選応援のため石川県入りし、国会で問題視された。簗和生前農水相を巡っても更迭の判断が後手に回り、参院では問責決議案の提出寸前に至った。16日の予算委で野党議員から「危機管理能力がない」と指摘されると、首相は色をなしてこう反論した。「24時間本当に常に公用スマホをそばに置いて大音量にして夜も横になっている」

title: PHPに欠陥 欧州各国でサイト遮断
body: 世界中で広く使われているプログラミング言語「PHP」に重大な欠陥が見つかったことを受けて、世界各国でもウェブサイトを一時遮断する動きが広がりました。フランスでは、パリ警視庁がデモに関する夜間外出禁止令を発表しているサイトにアクセスができなくなりました。また、フィンランド政府も一般向けウェブサイトを「予防措置」として遮断したと発表しました。オランダでは、ヨーロッパ最大の港であるロッテルダム港のサイトも遮断されました。イギリスの国家サイバーセキュリティーセンターは、修正プログラムが公開され次第、速やかに対応するように各組織に呼びかけるなど各国の政府が対応に追われています。

title: PHPの脆弱性 米OpenAIのAIで発見
body: 米OpenAIは10月21日（現地時間）、同日に修正版が公開されたオープンソースのプログラミング言語「PHP」の脆弱性について、OpenAIのAIモデルで発見したと発表した。「同様の発見は今後数カ月で急増する」と予測している。【OpenAI公式Xの発表全文】OpenAIによるオープンソースソフトウェアのセキュリティ支援プロジェクト「Patch the Planet」の一環で、セキュリティ企業の米CalifがAIモデル「GPT-5.6 Sol」を活用して発見した。OpenAIはパートナー企業や米政府などとも連携し、2カ月をかけてPHPの脆弱性と修正版を公開するための準備に協力した。なお、セキュリティ企業の米Wizも独自にこの脆弱性を発見した。同社によれば、GPT-5.6 Solに加え、米GoogleのAIモデル「Gemini 4 Argon」なども活用したという。OpenAIは、今回の脆弱性は攻撃者よりも先に最先端AIで発見できた一方、攻撃者もAIを悪用できると指摘する。またOpenAIでは他の重大な脆弱性への対応も進めており、「同様の発見は今後数カ月で急増する」と予測している。これを踏まえ、OpenAIは同社のセキュリティプログラムを通じた支援や、AIを前提とした脆弱性対策の枠組みの構築などに取り組むとしている。

title: メタに約4兆円支払い命令 米地裁
body: Diana Novak Jones[２１日 ロイター] - 米ニューメキシコ州の地裁は２１日、メタ・プラットフォームズに対し２５０億ドルの支払いを命じた。‌トランプ氏の２０１６年米大統領選陣営に関与した政治コンサルテ⁠ィング会社がフェイスブック利用者数百万人のデータを本人の同意なく取得したとされる問題を巡る訴訟で、州地裁​陪審がメタは利用者を欺いたと認定していた。ニューメキシコ州のラウル・トレス司法長官は、単独の州が‌企業を相手に勝ち取った判決として、米国史上最大級だと述べた。地裁のフランシス・マシュー判事は陪審評決を受けた‌命令で、この件は「フェイスブ‌ックの中核的な事業慣行そのものに関わる問​題だ」と指摘した。同判事は州法に基づけば２１９０億ドル超の制裁金が妥当と判断‌したが、２５０億ドルに減額した。メタのＣ・Ｊ・マホニー最高法務責任者（ＣＬＯ）は声明で、控訴審で勝訴する‌と確信していると表明した。同​氏は「今回の判断と司法長官による法執行の進め‌方は、ニューメキシコ州で事業を営むことを事実上不可能にする」と指摘。「⁠この訴訟は本質的に、人々がオンラインで何を発言できるかについて新たな規則を強制するため、言論に税を課そうとするものだ」と述べた。メタはこれま⁠で、数十億ドル規模の制裁金は、適正手続き​や過大な罰金からの保‌護を受ける憲法上の権利を侵害する恐れがあると主張していた。この件を巡っては、英政治コンサルティング会社ケンブリッジ・アナリテ⁠ィカがサードパーティー製アプリを通じて最大８７００万人分のフ⁠ェイスブック利用者の個人データを収集していたことが明らかになり、ニュ⁠ーメキシコ州の司法長官が２０２１年にメタを提訴していた。今回の制裁金は、ケンブリッジ・ア‌ナリ⁠ティカ問題を受けてメタに科されたものとしては最大とな​る。同社は１９年にも、同じ問題を巡り米連邦取引委員会（ＦＴＣ）から５０億ドルの制裁金を科された。

title: 米大統領 ウに露との和平合意促す
body: Steve Holland　Trevor Hunnicutt[ワシントン　２０日　ロイター] - トランプ米大統領は２０日、ロシアとの戦争終結に向け、ウクライナに和平合意に応‌じるよう求めた。トランプ氏はホワイトハウスの大統⁠領執務室で記者団に対し、「ウクライナはこの戦争を終わらせたいと望まなければならない」と述べた。また、「​ウクライナがこの戦争を終わらせるときが来た」とし、ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領が‌合意に応じることを望んでいると語った。その上で、ロシアは戦場で優位に立っているとの認識を表明。「ロシアは巨大‌な機械のようなもので、た‌だ前進し続けており、実際にそうしてき​た」とし、「ロシアは非常に広い領土を占領した」と述べた。トランプ氏はまた、‌ロシアで拘束されている米国人の元教師、スティーブン・ハバード氏の問題に‌ついて、ロシアのプーチン​大統領と協議したと明らかにし、この件につ‌いて近く進展がある可能性を示唆した。トランプ氏は、ハバード氏に関する⁠記者団の質問に対し「プーチン氏とこの件について話をしている」とし、「何が起きるか見ていてほしい。われわれはハバード氏の問題に集中⁠して取り組んできた」と述べた。ハバード氏は７４歳​で、傭兵活動に関‌する罪で有罪判決を受けロシアの刑務所で約７年の刑に服している。米国務省はハバード氏の件を不当拘束と認定している。ゼレンスキー⁠大統領はこの日、ノルウェーの首都オスロで米国⁠のウィットコフ和平交渉担当特使と会談。会談後の記者会見で、ロシア⁠による弾道ミサイル攻撃に関する情報共有や早期警戒の提供を米国が再開したこ‌とに⁠謝意を示した。ノルウェーのストーレ首相によると、ウィット​コフ氏は２１日にロシア第２の都市サンクトペテルブルクを訪問し、ロシア首脳部と会談する。

title: 露の道新記者拘束 米国務省が非難
body:
【ワシントン共同】米国務省の報道担当者は19日、ロシア当局がスパイ容疑で北海道新聞の記者を拘束したことを巡り「ジャーナリストや独立した意見を持つ人々に対する威嚇や嫌がらせ、処罰などのいかなる試みも非難する」と述べた。スパイ行為を否定する日本側を擁護した。共同通信の取材に答えた。【写真】「ロシア兵器9割に日本部品」　ミサイルや無人機に転用　名指しされた日本企業13社
報道担当者は「米国は表現の自由を基本的な権利と考えている。社会は自由な意見の表明により強化され、自由な社会での政府による検閲は容認できない」と訴えた。記者は13日、ウクライナへの「特別軍事作戦」に北方領土と千島列島から動員された兵士の数の情報を日本の情報機関の指示で収集したとしてロシア連邦保安局（FSB）に拘束された。

title: 米政権の汚職問題 中間選挙争点に
body:
間近に迫った米中間選挙の新たな争点にトランプ政権の「corruption（汚職、腐敗）」問題が急浮上している。最近の各種世論調査で、有権者がインフレやイラン戦争などより汚職問題を最も懸念していることが判明。メディアはこぞってこの話題を取り上げ、民主党は政権の汚職体質を有権者に訴える選挙CMを流し始めた。背景にあるのは「自分たちは物価高で苦しんでいるのに、大統領や周囲はその地位を利用して私腹を肥やしている」という国民の不満だ。今回の選挙は「左右」より「上下」の対立と言われるが、その構図が一段と鮮明になった。
The top five voter concerns are government corruption出典：Fox News　2026/10/14(水)
Democrats have made corruption a key midterm issue出典：MS NOW　2026/10/16(金)
トランプ大統領の純資産が1兆円を超えたという試算をアメリカの経済誌「フォーブス」が明らかにしました。出典：テレ朝NEWS　2026/9/18(金)
FOXニュースの調査では国民の約6割が「政府内の汚職」を「非常に懸念している」と述べ、インフレや移民問題などを上回り有権者の最大の懸念事項となった。トランプ氏に近いFOXの調査であることが、結果の信ぴょう性を高めている。
NBCニュースの調査では52%が「トランプ政権は過去の政権より腐敗している」と回答。ロイター通信の調査によると、共和党員も含めた国民の約7割がトランプ氏の私的な事業が大統領としての意思決定に影響を与えていると考えている。
ワシントン・ポスト紙は社説で「トランプ氏の家族や側近は富を蓄える一方、一般市民はインフレやガソリン価格の高騰に苦しんでいる」と批判。また「自身の支持者への恩赦や献金者への関税免除によって不正な資金提供の疑いを招いている」と大統領の汚職疑惑を指摘した。
フォーブス誌によるとトランプ大統領の直近の純資産は73億ドル。大統領選挙期間中の43億ドルの約70%増しだ。同誌は「米国史上いかなる大統領も、トランプほど地位を利用して巨額の利益を得た大統領はいない」と断じた。
こうしたトランプ氏の公私混同への国民の不満や批判が、自身の支持率低下と共和党のピンチを招いていることはほぼ間違いない。

title: 米国防長官 ネタニヤフ首相と会談
body: [エルサレム／ワシントン　２０日　ロイター] - ヘグセス米国防長官が１９日にイスラエルを電撃訪問し、ネタニヤフ首相とイラン情勢について協議した。イスラエル首相報道官‌が２０日、ロイターに対し明らかにした。ヘグセス氏もイスラエルを訪問し⁠たと確認したが、ネタニヤフ氏との非公開の会談の詳細について明らかにしなかった。イスラエルのシュピールマン首相報道官によると、ネタニヤフ首相はイスラエル南​部ネゲブ砂漠のウブダ空軍基地でヘグセス長官と会談。「地域の脅威」について協議し、その脅威に対し攻撃面と防衛面の双方で対処する米国とイ‌スラエルの協力について意見交換した。ヘグセス氏はイスラエルが米軍を受け入れていることに謝意を示したという。シュピールマン氏によると、駐留する米軍は数千人規模に上‌る。シュピールマン氏によると、両氏は‌トランプ米大統領によるネタニヤフ首相への支持についても意​見交換した。「両者の深い個人的関係が今回の協議の中心にあった」としている。ヘグセス氏はその後、ワシン‌トンで記者団に対し、イスラエルを訪問したと確認し「現地で米軍部隊を訪問し、その際に（ネタニヤフ）首相と話をす‌る機会があった」と語った。会談の​内容について話すことはないとし、「イスラエルが良きパートナーであ‌ることに感謝している」と述べるにとどめた。ヘグセス氏はこれに先立ち、ソーシャルメディアへの投稿で、中⁠東、北東アフリカ、アジアの一部を対象とする米中央軍の管轄域内で米軍将兵を訪問したと明らかにしていた。前日にはトランプ米大統領が、来週行われるイスラエル総選挙を巡りネタニヤフ氏への支持を表明。今⁠回の選挙は、２０２３年１０月７日のイスラム組織ハマスによるイスラエル奇襲攻撃​以降、初めてとなる。この攻撃‌を受けてイスラエルはパレスチナ自治区ガザ、レバノン、イランで戦闘を展開した。世論調査によると、ネタニヤフ氏率いる宗教・民族主義勢力の連立与党は過半数を失う見通しだ。ただ、野党側⁠も政権樹立に苦戦する可能性がある。バンス米副大統領は１９日、デジタルメディア「２ＷＡＹ」のインタ⁠ビューで、イスラエルの選挙には関与しないと述べ、ネタニヤフ氏への支持表明を控えた。「私が支持を表明す⁠るのは米国の候補者だ。私が注力しているのは中間選挙だ」と述べた。同氏は今年、ハンガリーのブダペストを‌訪問し、同国⁠の選挙でオルバン首相への支持を表明していた。バンス氏はネタニヤフ氏について、「​不支持を表明しているわけではないが、支持を表明しているわけでもない。イスラエルの選挙には関与しない」と語った。

title: PHPに欠陥 欧州各国でサイト遮断
body: 世界中で広く使われているプログラミング言語「PHP」に重大な欠陥が見つかったことを受けて、世界各国でもウェブサイトを一時遮断する動きが広がりました。フランスでは、パリ警視庁がデモに関する夜間外出禁止令を発表しているサイトにアクセスができなくなりました。また、フィンランド政府も一般向けウェブサイトを「予防措置」として遮断したと発表しました。オランダでは、ヨーロッパ最大の港であるロッテルダム港のサイトも遮断されました。イギリスの国家サイバーセキュリティーセンターは、修正プログラムが公開され次第、速やかに対応するように各組織に呼びかけるなど各国の政府が対応に追われています。

title: EVの補助金引き下げ 27年1月から
body: 経済産業省は10月21日、電気自動車（EV）などの購入を補助する「クリーンエネルギー自動車導入促進補助金（CEV補助金）」について、補助額を見直すと発表した。補助額を現在の6～8割ほどに抑える。2027年1月1日以降に新車として登録を受ける車両に対し、見直し後の補助額を適用する。1月からのCEV補助金対象車種一覧見直し後の補助上限額は、EVが125万円から75万円、軽EVが55万円から44万円、プラグインハイブリッド車が80万円から48万円、燃料電池車が145万円から87万円となる（グリーン鋼材の採用計画などGXの取り組みを評価する加算額を除く）。GXの加算は、最大5万円から同3万円（軽EVは最大3万円から同1.8万円）へ見直す。見直しを受け、EVでは車種ごとの補助額が現行の6割となる。例えばトヨタ自動車の「bZ4X」の補助額はGXの加算を含め130万円から78万円に、テスラの「モデル3」は127万円から76万2000円に引き下げられる。一方、軽EVの減額割合には6割～8割と幅を設ける。スズキの「eスカイ」は56万8000円から45万円に、比亜迪（BYD）の「ラッコ」は15万円から9万円に見直される。経産省は9月、CEV補助金の申請受け付け終了時期が12月上旬～下旬となる見込みであることをウェブサイト上で公表。補助期間に空白が生じることが懸念されていた。仮に現行予算を使い切っても、次年度予算を元にした遡及（そきゅう）適用などを含め、財務省と調整して財源を手当てし、切れ目なく補助金を出す考え。

title: SpaceXとテスラ 経営統合を検討
body: 米実業家イーロン・マスク氏は20日、自身が率いる米宇宙開発企業スペースXと米電気自動車（EV）大手テスラの経営統合の可能性を検討する特別委員会を設置したと明らかにした。欧米メディアが伝えた。マスク氏は両社の統合について「良いアイデア」と発言した。【写真まとめ】夜空に次々と現れたスターリンク衛星のフレア◇「シンギュラリティーの段階にある」この日のスペースXの決算説明会で言及した。報道によると、マスク氏は人工知能（AI）について「（人間の知能を超える）シンギュラリティーの段階にある」とした上で、両社の統合で得られるものは多いとの認識を示した。経営統合は「良いアイデアだと思うが、最終的には株主が支持しなければならない」と述べ、委員会はまだ合意に至っていないと強調した。◇マスク氏自身は議論に参加せずテスラ側は投票した株主だけでなく、全株主の50％の賛成票が必要になると指摘し、「かなり高いハードルだ」とした。マスク氏自身は利害関係にある当事者であるため、いずれの取締役会の議論にも参加していないという。【ワシントン浅川大樹】

title: 米ネトフリ純利益44%増 7～9月期
body:
【ニューヨーク共同】米動画配信大手ネットフリックスが20日発表した2026年7～9月期決算は、純利益が前年同期比44％増の36億6392万ドル（約5800億円）、売上高は12％増の128億7417万ドルだった。料金の値上げや、世界的な会員数の増加が業績拡大に寄与した。【写真】中国企業に買われた「東芝ブランド」その後　19年
ただ、同時に公表した10～12月期の売上高の伸び率は4四半期連続で減速する見込み。ロイター通信によると純利益見通しも市場予想を下回ったとして、成長鈍化への警戒感から同社の株価は時間外取引で一時7％近く急落した。ネットフリックスはユーチューブや動画投稿アプリ「TikTok」などとの視聴時間を巡る競争に直面している。

title: フラット35 全国で不適正利用64件
body: 長期固定金利型住宅ローン「フラット35」の融資審査について会計検査院が調べたところ、民泊施設や店舗として利用する不適正利用が計64件あったことが判明した。【図解】住宅はいま「売り時」で「買い時」?　金利上昇懸念の影響フラット35では、各金融機関が審査したうえで利用者に住宅購入資金を融資する。独立行政法人「住宅金融支援機構」は、金融機関からローン債権を買い取る証券化支援を実施するなど、住宅ローンの供給を支援することで国民の住宅取得を後押ししている。利用者は融資が受けやすくなる一方、購入した物件を事業で使わず、居住することなどが要件として求められる。検査院は2023～24年度に融資対象となった全国の5万4221件のうち、都市部の戸建て住宅を抽出調査。その結果、64件（融資額計30億4074万円）の不適正利用が発覚した。届け出をせずに住宅の一部を店舗などに利用したのが39件、民泊などに利用したのが25件だった。東京都豊島区の3階建ての新築戸建てでは、ローン利用者が8000万円の融資を受けたが、検査院が確認したところ、利用者は居住せず、物件を無許可で旅館業施設として使っていたことが発覚。この利用者の勤務先は、複数の旅館業施設を運営する会社だった。検査院は、64件のローン利用者が適切な対応を取らなければ全額繰り上げ償還などを求めるよう機構に要請。また、金融機関の融資審査時点で住宅の間取りを確認したり、民泊の届け出状況を確認したりする対応も求める。【山田豊】

title: 北海道職員が「就活セクハラ」か
body: 学生が参加する北海道主催のインターンシップで、道の男性職員が女子学生に交際を迫るなど不適切な連絡を繰り返していたことが20日、毎日新聞の取材で判明した。就職活動中の女子学生が被害に遭う「就活セクハラ」に該当する可能性があるとして、道は男性の処分を検討している。【図解でわかる】当てはまる？令和時代のハラスメント道によると、インターンは8～9月、道に就職を希望する大学生らを対象に開催し、計291人が参加。セクハラ行為が疑われている男性職員は所属部局でインターンに参加した学生の指導などを担当していた。男性職員は8月のインターンに参加した女子学生とLINE（ライン）の連絡先を交換。女子学生にメッセージを送り、食事に誘うなどした。女子学生は断ったが、男性職員はさらに連絡を重ねたという。女子学生が道の担当部局に相談して問題が発覚。道は女子学生に謝罪し、男性職員をインターン担当から外した。道は「事実関係を調査中」として、20日現在で男性職員を処分していない。男性職員は女子学生に対する行為についておおむね認めているという。道人事課の担当者は毎日新聞の取材に対し「参加した学生の期待を裏切る行為。再発防止に努めたい」とコメントした。【小林大輝】

title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
summary: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
body:
Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.
The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.
Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."
The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", andZelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisangroup of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.
Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
summary: President Vladimir Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war, the BBC's Russia Editor writes.
body:
Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
summary: The comment is an apparent swipe at Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump, who both face elections in coming weeks.
body:
Protesters rallied in Lille along with other cities across the country
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the  riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.
Clean up begins after French riots but police remain
Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters
Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...
"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in aninterview for Israel's i24 channel,externalthat France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".
He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.
Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.
"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."
"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.
Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters
Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
Pink Panther rioting in France is actually AI
According to areport in the UK's Financial Times newspaper,external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.
It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.
Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.
David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".
France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.
BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.
The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.
The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.
Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.
The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.
It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.
While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.
Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
summary: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.
body:
Pope Leo returned to St Peter's Square on Wednesday for his weekly general audience
Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.
Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.
"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.
The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.
It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.
The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.
The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".
Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.
On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".
The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.
Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

title: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken
summary: Locals describe the MP, who had to have both legs amputated, as a genuinely kind person who fought for the community.
body:
Wangaratta locals have described their disbelief at the alleged attack on local MP Helen Haines
Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival.
Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people.
They are clearly in shock about what police say wasa targeted and deliberate attackon Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office.
"People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday.
The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said.
The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted.
"Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a giftware shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit.
"She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family."
Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm andappeared in courton Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder.
Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant says Helen Haines is a "cheerful" and "committed" MP
First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission.
She was spurred on by a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people.
The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government.
Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities.
On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician.
Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights.
In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police whentwo officers were shot deadin the nearby town of Porepunkah last year.
Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured.
"It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids."
"To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added.
"She just thanked everyone."
Bystanders Jacob Evans, Cody Lepoidevin and Jacklyn Black said Haines thanked them for rushing to her aid
There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away.
Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!"
It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other.
Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside,he rushed to help, pinning down the suspect.
"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident.
"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way."
Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you".
Floral tributes to Helen Haines have mounted up outside her office
Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines.
Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines".
Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support.
"I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter."
"Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury.
"It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here."
With additional reporting by Simon Atkinson

title: The "trillion pound" oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
summary: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
body:
The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig in the North Sea.
After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.
Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.
A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.
It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?
It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.
"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.
"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."
On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.
The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.
"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.
It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.
Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.
The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.
Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.
The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.
I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.
Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.
It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.
While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.
UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.
Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.
Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?
How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?

title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
summary: The vulnerabilities with PHP, a programming language widely used across the internet, have been described as the most significant ever found by AI.
body:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agencyissued similar advice on X,externalfor organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
Andin a post on X,external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are "temporarily down for maintenance,external" without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz.
Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet.
Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.
OpenAI saidin a blog post,externalthat the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.
The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," theNCSC said in a note,external.
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officialshave issued a similar warning,external.
"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare,said he was,external"seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
body:
Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.
A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".
Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.
The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an$18bn deal with Californiaover child safety.
New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.
New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.
Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.
Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.
They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday.
"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."
The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.
Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.
He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.
Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.
While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.
It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.
Campaigners welcome Meta and YouTube's defeat in landmark social media addiction trial
Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant
New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this yearalso fined Meta almost $1bnfor misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.
The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".
As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.
Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people.
"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.
To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.
The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.
Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.
Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.
Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock.
Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
summary: The updated policy will apply to all reservations booked on the accommodation site on or after 20 November.
body:
Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.
Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.
The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.
"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".
The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.
A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and  will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.
Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.
If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.
Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.
TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.
One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.
They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted
Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

title: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroad
summary: With graduate jobs hard to come by, more young adults are reported to be considering emigrating.
body:
Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseas
Last year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place.
"I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."
More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to asurvey,externalof 15,000 final year university students.
Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high.
UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago,according to the ISE's report,external.
For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?
While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad,official figures show.,external
In addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under itsWorking Holiday Maker programme,,externalBritish passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.
Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than London
Rachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for insurance giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.
She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.
Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched.
"People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."
Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to themost recent figures,externalfrom the UK's Office for National Statistics.
It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.
After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.
Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunities
Charlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.
West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching.
"I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live.
"In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."
The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.
One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.
Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from Finland
This is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.
Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020.
"Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."
Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon.
"To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."
Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas.
"When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."
Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London.
"I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."

title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
summary: The UK government says the field, which is opposed by environmental campaigners, could be producing gas by the end of this month.
body:
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she toldBBC Radio Scotland Breakfastthat it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".
"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.
The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.
She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.
"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.
The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".
He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".
Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.
The Jackdaw platform is located east of Aberdeen
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.
"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.
He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".
Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."
Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.
Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?
But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled thatconsent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
BBC News visited the Jackdaw platform this summer
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCullochsaid its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortagesthis winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.
In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy MinisterMichael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined,external.
"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
UK government approves drilling in Jackdaw gas field with production to start this month
Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields?
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
summary: While not naming the disgraced former MP, the Metropolitan Police has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.
body:
Donaldson arriving at Newry Crown Court for a previous court appearance in June
Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.
The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.
Last weekDonaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prisonfor a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.
It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.
The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.
While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.
It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.
"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.
"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."
In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.
She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.
On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.
But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.
Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in Londonwere raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year.
A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.
Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
summary: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.
These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.
Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.
But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.
During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving thegreen light to the Jackdaw gas fieldin the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".
He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".
No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firmNesta that they could be moved to the unit rate,external, so people pay for what they use.
This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.
For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.
Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.
Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.
When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.
Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.
The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.
Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, butCitizens Advice has warned,externalabout the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.
Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.
But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."
Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy pricesforecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January.
In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".
Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy
summary: Number 10 North deputy director Duncan Parish has told a conference he is still facing "institutional barriers".
body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened Number 10 North in July
A "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said.
Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.
The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.
Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.
Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".
Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care.
"But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.
He said onepriority of Number 10 Northwas to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.
Duncan Parish spoke to local political and business leaders in Lincolnshire, in an event chaired by regional mayor Dame Andrea Jenkyns
Describing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance."
He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow".
"But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said.
"We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down."
His comments come as the government continues to face questions about thecost to the taxpayerof the new headquarters.
In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick".
"The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.
He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.
Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.
The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.
Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, andhosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September.
Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?
"Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place."
